headline: Mi, “body”, is from Proto-Japonic *muy and cognate with 実 (mi, “seed, fruit, offspring”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *muy. Cognate with 実 (mi, “seed, fruit, offspring”).
Standalone form of mu below. See also the etymology of 神 (kami, kamu).
Compare Korean 몸 (mom, “body”).

headline: Pikapika was written fikafika in a 1595 Latin–Portuguese–Japanese dictionary, a reduplication of the root of 光る (hikaru).

sources.quote: /fikafika/ → /pikapika/
First attested as ひかひか (fikafika) in the 1595 Dictionarivm Latino Lvsitanicvm, ac Iaponicvm (“Dictionary from Latin into Portuguese, and Japanese”).
Reduplication of the ひか (hika-) root of Old Japanese-derived verb 光る (hikaru, “to shine, to gleam”), which root is from Proto-Japonic *pika. See also *pikaru.

As part of the Late Middle Japanese reintroduction of /p/ as a phoneme, particularly among mimetic words and in some Sino-Japanese compounds, this word regained its original /p/ sound that had by then shifted to /ɸ/.

headline: Yokubari is the stem of 欲張る (yokubaru, “to be intensely greedy”) and appears in texts from 1813.

sources.quote: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 欲張る (yokubaru, “to be intensely greedy”).

Ultimately, likely a shift from older synonym 欲ぼり (yokubori), dating to 1519.

headline: Yudan is “unclear, with multiple theories”, one drawing on the story of a pot of oil (油鉢) in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.

sources.quote: Unclear, with multiple theories.
* From the story of the 油鉢 (yuhatsu, “pot of oil”) in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (大般涅槃経); see 大般涅槃経#油断大敵.
* Sound change from 寛(ゆた)に (yuta ni).
* There is a lamp in Enryaku-ji (延暦寺) that has been alight since the time of Saichō (最澄), its founder, and 油断 (literally “oil + end”) refers to not letting it go out.
The term is not understood in other parts of the Sinosphere.

morphemes.meaning: to gain, to become; to attach to, to be connected with, to come in contact with

sources.quote: From 思(おも)い (omoi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 思(おも)う (omou, “to think, to imagine”).) + 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to gain, to become; to attach to, to be connected with, to come in contact with”).

headline: Hotoke, “Buddha”, most likely comes from Proto-Koreanic *Pwutukye, related to modern Korean 부처 (Bucheo).

sources.quote: *⟨poto₂ke₂⟩ → */pətəkəi̯/ → /ɸotoke/ → /hotoke/

From Old Japanese, most likely from Proto-Koreanic *Pwutukye, hence related to modern Korean 부처 (Bucheo), Manchu ᡶᡠᠴᡳᡥᡳ (fucihi); see the Proto-Korean entry for more. The word was presumably disseminated by the Baekje people of southwestern Korea, who first introduced Buddhism to Japan. The first two syllables are ultimately from Sanskrit बुद्ध (buddhá), via Middle Chinese 佛陀 (MC bjut da) or some similar Sinitic form. Thomas Pellard speculates that the final element is an ancient Koreanic word for "king; lord".

The more traditional explanation still given in Japanese dictionaries is that the final ke element might be the Chinese-derived suffix 気(け) (ke, “spirit”), but a Koreanic explanation is more plausible.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

headline: Daibubun is 大 (dai, “big, great”) plus 部分 (bubun, “part, portion”), first attested in 1903.

sources.quote: Compound of 大 (dai, “big, great”) + 部分 (bubun, “part, portion”).

headline: Waki began as a noun from 分く (waku, “to split, to divide”): the space where two things split apart, then “side”.

sources.quote: Nominalization of verb 分く (waku, “to split, to divide”), from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, continuative stem), 分き (waki). Came to refer to the space between where two things split off from each other, and then, by extension, came to refer to the side of something.

headline: Takara, “treasure”, was analyzed as 高 (taka-, “high”) plus a pluralizing suffix, but the page calls that semantically problematic.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshū of 759 CE. From Proto-Japonic *takara.

Samuel Martin analyzes this as a compound of 高(たか) (taka-, “high”) + 等(ら) (-ra, pluralizing suffix). However, this is semantically problematic, as such a compound would ordinarily refer to “the heights” as a location, and there is no clear means of deriving the sense of “treasure” from the proposed component parts.

Some sources derive this as a compound of 田(た) (ta, “paddy field”) + から (kara, “from”), literally “from the paddy fields”, from the way people value thriving paddy fields as a unique kind of treasure. However, the sense of “from” for から (kara) does not appear until roughly the Heian period, more recent than the first appearance of takara, making this a folk etymology.
